input: In the realm of refrigeration engineering, the performance of a vapour-compression system can be better understood by comparing it against the ideal Carnot benchmark, and this example explores that comparison for a unit serving an ice rink. The unit in question operates with an evaporating temperature of −25 °C and a condensing temperature of 35 °C, and it is worth noting that these two temperatures define the window within which the refrigeration cycle operates. The coefficient of performance, which serves as the key measure of efficiency for such systems, expresses the amount of heat removed relative to the work consumed. When the temperatures are converted to the absolute scale, the evaporating temperature becomes 248.15 K while the condensing temperature becomes 308.15 K, giving a temperature difference of 60 K across the cycle. Leveraging the Carnot relationship, which divides the evaporating temperature by this difference (248.15 / 60), the Carnot coefficient of performance is calculated as 4.13, representing the theoretical maximum that no real machine operating between the same temperatures can surpass. By contrast, the installed unit achieves a coefficient of performance of just 1.45, a figure obtained from the manufacturer's full-load test data, highlighting the gap between idealised performance and real-world operation. It is reassuring that 1.45 sits below the Carnot ceiling of 4.13, as any higher value would indicate an error somewhere in the data. Furthermore, it should be emphasised that part-load performance is not stated by the manufacturer, meaning that the comparison between the achieved value and the benchmark value of 4.13 is strictly valid only at full load and at the specified operating temperatures, underscoring the importance of understanding the conditions attached to published performance figures.
target: A vapour-compression unit serves an ice rink, evaporating at −25 °C and condensing at 35 °C. Calculate the Carnot coefficient of performance (COP) between the two temperatures, and set the installed unit against it. The COP of a refrigerator is the heat removed at the evaporator divided by the work input; it is a ratio of two energy flows and carries no unit. The refrigerant boils in the evaporator and takes up heat from the rink side at the evaporating temperature; it condenses and rejects heat at the condensing temperature. The unit therefore lifts heat across the interval between the two temperatures, and the size of that interval, with the lower temperature, fixes the best performance any refrigerator can reach between them. On the absolute scale, the evaporating temperature is 248.15 K and the condensing temperature is 308.15 K, a difference of 60 K. The Carnot COP is the evaporating temperature divided by the difference between the two absolute temperatures, 248.15 / 60 = 4.13. The Carnot COP is the COP of a reversible refrigerator between the same temperatures, and no real unit working between them exceeds it. The installed unit achieves a COP of 1.45, well below the Carnot limit of 4.13, and the comparison passes the check that the achieved value must fall under the reversible limit. The difference between the achieved COP and the Carnot COP is the cost of the irreversibilities in the real cycle, which the reversible cycle does not carry. The achieved figure is from the manufacturer's test of the unit at full load. Part-load performance is not stated, and no COP at part load is given here: the comparison between 1.45 and 4.13 holds at full load and at the stated temperatures, and at no other condition.
